knownFor: Spanish lay teacher of a strict ascetic life, made bishop of Abila, who was condemned by bishops and put to death by the emperor Maximus, and was then honored by his followers as a martyr.
datesNote: Sulpicius Severus says he was condemned at Saragossa, which he denied; put to death at Trèves under Maximus; Ernest Cushing Richardson dates him flourished 379, died 385
placeNote: Spain; bishop of Abila; executed at Trèves
role: Lay teacher, then bishop of Abila

keyWorks.title: Liber apologeticus (Tractate I)
keyWorks.about: his defense of his faith, cursing the Patripassians, the Manichaeans and other heresies

keyWorks.title: Liber ad Damasum episcopum (Tractate II)

traces: After his death, Sulpicius Severus says, his followers honored him as a martyr, and "it came to be thought the highest exercise of religion to swear by Priscillian."
A council at Braga in 561 still cursed teachings it named as his, among them that souls sinned in heaven and were cast down into bodies.
Sulpicius says the quarrel that followed was kept up for fifteen years and "could not by any means be set at rest."

At the First Council of Toledo, held in about 400, the bishops heard that clergy of the bishop Herenas had cried out, unasked, that Priscillian was a catholic and a holy martyr, and that Herenas held to the end that he was catholic and had suffered persecution from the bishops.

Sulpicius says Ithacius, the chief accuser, was the only one of those who had acted against Priscillian who was thrust out of the episcopate, and that Ydacius resigned his bishopric of his own accord.

In 447 Leo, bishop of Rome, wrote to a bishop in Spain against the Priscillianists. He said the rulers of the world so abhorred this folly that they laid low its originator, with most of his disciples, "by the sword of the public laws", and that this rigorous treatment was for long a help to the church's law of gentleness.
A law of 407 names the Priscillianists, with the Manichaeans and Phrygians, among those the emperors pursue with the most deserved severity.
remembered: Sulpicius calls him "a man of noble birth, of great riches, bold, restless, eloquent, learned through much reading."
Jerome of Strido says he "published many short writings, some of which have reached us."

uncertain: His teaching comes to us mostly through his enemies. Sulpicius Severus thought him a Gnostic heretic, and was just as hostile to his accusers, Ithacius of Sossuba and Ydacius of Emerita. Orosius, a Spanish priest who wrote to Augustine of Hippo against the Priscillianists, says he taught that souls came down from God through circles of evil powers into bodies. Long after, in 561, the council at Braga cursed like teachings in his name. Jerome of Strido reports that some accused him of Gnosticism and his defenders denied it.
Sulpicius says the council at Saragossa condemned Priscillian in his absence. Priscillian, in his book to Damasus, says no one of his group was accused, convicted or condemned there.

Sulpicius says Priscillian did not deny that he had given himself up to lewd teachings, held night meetings with women and prayed naked. These were the findings of the court of Evodius, and Sulpicius gives no account from Priscillian's side.
The eleven Würzburg treatises carry no author's name. Georg Schepss, who found them in 1885 and printed them in 1889, judged from the names in the first two that they could only be Priscillian's.
Alexander Roberts's English Sulpicius says he was made bishop "in the town of Arles". Halm's Latin reads Abilensi oppido, the town of Abila, as Jerome also has it.
Ernest Cushing Richardson's English Jerome says Priscillian "belonged to the party of Hydatius and Ithacius". Sulpicius names these two as his accusers.
The sources used here give no year of birth, parents or schooling. Sulpicius reports that "it was believed that he had practised magical arts from his boyhood."

The year of his death is not fixed. Richardson's note to Jerome gives 385. Fremantle's table of dates for Jerome gives 386, and Hydatius places the deaths under a later year, which his editor Mommsen marks 387. The story says in about 385.

Whether his death was the first execution of a Christian for heresy rests on editors alone, and no primary source held says so. The note to Theodoret by Blomfield Jackson speaks of "the first capital punishment of a heretic", and Fremantle's table of dates for Jerome lists "386. Execution of Priscillian for heresy at Treves." Hefele, in Oxenham's English, reports the view of Bernays, who holds against the general view that the charges were sorcery ("maleficium") and night meetings for prayer, and that Priscillian and his followers "were not executed for heresy." In Sulpicius the prefect Evodius convicts him of "evil conduct" in Roberts's English; the Latin word is maleficium, sorcery. The story gives the verdict as the court's.

Where Roberts's English and Halm's Latin differ, the story follows the Latin. Roberts says the trial was put off "as long as Martin survived"; the Latin says it was put off while Martin was at Trier. Roberts says a war of quarreling went on "between them and our friends"; the Latin says among our own people (inter nostros), which puts it on Sulpicius's side. Hydatius's Chronicle says Martin and other bishops judged Priscillian a heretic in Gaul, while Sulpicius has Martin beg Maximus not to shed blood.

No held source dates Sulpicius's Chronicle. The story says he wrote some years after the deaths because he says the quarrel after them had gone on for fifteen years; that is an inference from his words.

Sulpicius says Ithacius alone was thrust out of the episcopate and that Ydacius resigned. Prosper's Chronicle says that in 389 the bishops Ithacius and Ursacius were cut off from the church's communion for the killing of Priscillian, whose accusers they had been.

Sulpicius says that on the way to Rome the party lingered for a little while "in the territory of Euchrotia", and that Euchrotia was beheaded with Priscillian. Prosper calls her the wife of the rhetorician Delphidius.

Sulpicius traces the teaching to Marcus of Memphis, through Agape and the rhetorician Helpidius, and says the bishops Instantius and Salvianus bound themselves to Priscillian "with a kind of oath". He says the bishop Ydacius harassed them "without measure" and only fanned the fire. Priscillian's own book denies the heresies and curses them. Sulpicius also says that after Damasus and Ambrose turned them away, the party won over Macedonius, master of the offices, "by bribery and flattery" and recovered their churches; Priscillian says Ydacius had won his rescript by a false petition that hid their names.

The first of the Würzburg tractates, the Liber apologeticus, says whoever uses magic rites with first fruits and an ointment cursed to the Sun and the Moon is to be pursued with the sword, and says that if it could be done the author would send Mani's followers to the underworld by the sword. Schepss's attribution of the tractates to Priscillian is the only one held.

Jerome, in a later letter, speaks of him as "condemned by the whole world and put to death by the secular sword". Augustine says that real Priscillianists, posing as Catholics, "execrate the Priscillianists' false martyrdoms".

The First Council of Toledo is held in one print only, Mansi's, in a long-s scan. Professions of faith in it, under the names of the bishops Symphosius and Dictinius, condemn Priscillian's books with their author, but an editor's note in Mansi doubts they belong to this council, since they call both men bishops of holy memory.

Mansi's note quotes Ambrose as saying that the emperor, seeing him keep away from the bishops in communion with him, or those who sought the death of some, though they had strayed from the faith, was angered and ordered him to leave without delay. The note is the only held place for this, and its scan is damaged.

briefReferences: Priscillian's book to Damasus (Tractate II), ed. Georg Schepss: the call to give up parents, children, wealth and rank for God; why he and his friends gave themselves wholly to God after baptism; his creed and his curse on every heresy, the Manichaeans above all; what he says of Saragossa and of Damasus's own letter against judging the absent and unheard; his reason for going to Rome. It opens the story and closes it.
Schepss's preface: the eleven unsigned treatises found at Würzburg in 1885, and his judgment that they could be no one's but Priscillian's.

Sulpicius Severus, Chronicle II.46-51, in Roberts's English and Halm's Latin: the portrait, the belief in magic from boyhood, the two accounts of Saragossa, the bishopric of Abila, Gratian's order, Damasus and Ambrose turning the party away, Maximus at Trier, the appeal at Bordeaux, Ithacius's charge against readers and fasters, Martin's plea, the prefect's two hearings and their findings, the deaths, the martyr's cult, the quarrel among his own side, and Ithacius's loss of his bishopric. The line "My own view is that the accused displease me as much as the accusers." is his.
Hefele's History of the Councils, reporting Bernays: the charge of maleficium glossed as sorcery.
First Council of Toledo, in Mansi's collection: the clergy who called him a catholic and a holy martyr.
Leo the Great, Letter 15 to Turribius, tr. Charles Lett Feltoe: the sword of the public laws.
First Council of Braga, in Bruns: the curse on teachings it named as his, among them that souls sinned in heaven and were cast down into bodies.
Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, ch. 121, tr. Richardson: bishop of Abila, put to death at Trier by Maximus, and the dating note.
World census, Priscillian asceticism: his tradition.

quotationOriginals.modern: No one should be forbidden, if he despises parents, children, wealth and rank, even his own life, and would rather love God than the world.
quotationOriginals.printed: nee prohibere si quis contemptis parenti- T)us liberis facultatibus dignitate et adhuc et aiiima sua deum malluerit amare quam saeculum
quotationOriginals.work: Priscillian, Book to Damasus (Tractate II), Latin, ed. Georg Schepss
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Schepss's print is the only one held, and the scan misreads letters: nee for nec, T)us for the end of parentibus, aiiima for anima, and a stray mark after deum. No second print confirms the reading, so the Latin is given as the scan stands and not as an original; the rendering follows the sense of the sentence. malluerit is the manuscript's spelling.

quotationOriginals.modern: My own view is that the accused displease me as much as the accusers.
quotationOriginals.printed: And my feeling indeed is, that the accusers were as distasteful to me as the accused.
quotationOriginals.work: Sulpicius Severus, Chronicle II.50, tr. Alexander Roberts
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Halm's Latin (lines 5890-5891 of the Halm file) is held only in a damaged scan that reads senteatia and dispUcere, so it is not printed. The story renders the Latin, mea quidem sententia est, mihi tam reos quam accusatores displicere, which puts the accused first; Roberts puts the accusers first.

quotationOriginals.modern: Even the rulers of the world loathed this unholy folly. So they cut down its founder, with most of his followers, by the sword of the public laws.
quotationOriginals.printed: for even the leaders of the world so abhorred this profane folly that they laid low its originator, with most of his disciples, by the sword of the public laws.
quotationOriginals.work: Leo the Great, Letter 15 to Turribius, tr. Charles Lett Feltoe, 1895
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Leo's Latin is not held. The story splits Feltoe's one sentence in two and uses rulers for his leaders, unholy for profane, cut down for laid low, founder for originator and followers for disciples.
